source_text:
ART. II.
De duplici materiae causalitate & potentia; item de formarum eductione ex potentia materiae.

1. In hoc articulo notandum est primo, Materiam seu causam materialem, duplicem habere causalitatem; unam respectu compositi, seu materiati, alteram respectu formarum ab ea pendentium. Causalitas ejus respectu compositi est in eo posita, quod tanquam pars essentialis constituat compositum: respectu formarum ab ea pendentium, causalitas ejus in eo est posita, quod concursu passivo concurrat cum agente ad tribuendum iis esse, & ad illud ipsum esse conservandum.

2. Secundo notandum est, duplicem esse materiae potentiam, unam receptivam tantum, & non etiam causativam, alteram & receptivam & causativam. Priorem potentiam habet materia respectu solius animae rationalis; habet enim potentiam naturalem recipiendi animam in se, sed non habet potentiam concurrendi in genere causae materialis, ad tribuendum esse animae: posteriorem habet respectu omnium aliarum formarum, tum essentialium, tum accidentalium: non solum enim potest eas recipere in se, sed etiam concursu passivo cooperari cum agente, ad eas producendas.

3. Tertio notandum est, illos Philosophos male explicare eductionem formarum ex potentia materiae, qui dicunt formam actu existere in materia, ante rei generationem, non tamen apparere, sed quasi sub confusione potentiae ejus latitare, per generationem vero manifestam fieri, ita ut illud esse actuale, quod prius erat quasi absconditum, non incipiat simpliciter per generationem, sed per eam incipiat fieri manifestum, & sic e tenebris ac confusione materiae, quasi in lucem educatur. Dico hanc explicationem eductionis malam esse, quia si forma existat actu in materia ante compositi generationem, ipsum compositum existit ante suam generationem; quod aperte absurdum est: ratio consequentiae est, quia ex materia & forma actu existentibus, & unitis, resultat compositum, iisque positis necessario ponitur compositum; ideoque si materia & forma existant unitae, ante generationem compositi, ipsum compositum existit ante suam generationem. Dicet aliquis: si forma non existit in materia ante rei generationem, non potest dici ex materia educi, seu extrahi: nihil enim potest educi, seu extrahi ex eo, in quo non est. Resp. Formam dici ex materia educi, non quod ex materiae substantia, sed quod ex materiae potentia causativa educatur seu extrahatur: quamvis enim forma ante generationem in ipsa materiae substantia non existat, in ejus tamen potentia vere & proprie existere dicitur, quatenus a materia est producibilis; nam esse in materiae potentia causativa, nihil est aliud, nisi a materia tanquam a principio passivo posse produci.

4. Quarto notandum est, illos etiam toto caelo errare, qui dicunt formas, ante generationem, secundum esse inchoatum & imperfectum, h.e. secundum gradus quosdam suae entitatis, existere in materia: per generationem vero incipere esse in materia, secundum esse completum, & consummatum. Dico hujus sententiae Patronos turpiter errare, quia inde sequitur formam substantialem variari, quoad gradus intensionis & remissionis, non minus quam accidentia; quia item absurdum est, in una & eadem materia actu existere omnes formas, quae ex materiae potentia educi possunt, sive sint totales, sive partiales; sic enim in una & eadem re, simul essent pene infinitae entitates substantiales & diversae. Sed objiciet aliquis: si forma ante rei generationem plane nihil sit, sequetur omnes formas fieri ex nihilo, & proinde creari. Resp. Formas omnes posse dici fieri ex nihilo, si fieri ex nihilo accipiatur pro fieri ex nulla sui parte praeexistente, non vero si fieri ex nihilo accipiatur proprie, pro eo quod est fieri ex nulla materia praeexistente, quo sensu idem valet ac creari: fiunt enim formae ex materia, h.e. fiunt materia concurrente in genere causae subjectivae, ad tribuendum iis esse.

5. Quinto notandum est, eos etiam male explicare eductionem formarum ex materiae potentia, qui dicunt formam ideo ex materiae potentia educi, quod materia ante adventum formae habeat potentiam ad eam recipiendam: Si enim haec explicatio esset veritati consentanea, omnes formae, nulla excepta, essent ex materiae potentia educibiles; idque quia materia habet potentiam ad quamlibet formam recipiendam, potentiam (inquam) vel naturalem, vel obedientialem. Potentia autem naturalis est ea, quae educibilis est in actum vi alicujus agentis naturalis, ut potentia passiva ligni ad recipiendum calorem, dicitur naturalis, quia educi potest in actum vi naturalis agentis, ignis videlicet. Potentia materiae obedientialis est, quae in actum educi non potest vi agentis naturalis, sed vi alicujus agentis superioris, atque alterius ordinis, cui ea materia ita subdita est, & subjecta, ut necessario ei obediat: talis est potentia ligni, vel lapidis ad formam statuae; non enim educitur in actum vi alicujus agentis naturalis, sed vi agentis per artem: talis etiam est potentia animae ad recipienda dona supernaturalia, ut fidem, spem, charitatem, non enim ulla vi naturali in actum educi potest, sed infinita vi & virtute creatoris.

6. His positis: facile est explicare eductionem formarum ex materiae potentia; cum enim nihil possit educi ex aliquo, nisi illud quod prius fuit in eo; manifestum est eas solas formas ex potentia causativa materiae educi, quae antequam existant, sunt in potentia causativa materiae, i.e. producibiles sunt per concursum passivum materiae: illae enim formae quamdiu actu non existunt, habent potentiam ad accipiendum esse a materia, tanquam a principio passivo & receptivo; ideoque cum actu existere incipiunt, vi activa agentis, & passiva materiae, recte dicuntur educi ex potentia causativa materiae, quia non amplius sunt in potentia causativa materiae, i.e. non jam sunt a materia producibiles; quod enim semel productum & causatum est, non amplius est in potentia causae, sed eductum est ex statu potentialitatis, in statum actualitatis. Forma igitur bruti vere dicitur educi ex potentia causativa materiae seminis, quia ante generationem bruti, illa forma fuit in potentia causativa materiae seminis, i.e. producibilis erat vi passiva istius materiae; jam vero per actionem generantis, illa forma producta est, & posita extra potentiam causativam materiae; ita ut non amplius sit producibilis vi passiva materiae, nisi amittat eam existentiam, quam nunc habet. Contra vero anima humana, licet producatur in materia: non tamen ex ejus potentia causativa educitur, sed in materiam inducitur, idque quia nunquam fuit in materiae potentia causativa, nec materia unquam habuit potentiam ad tribuendum esse animae, per passivum suum concursum.
english: Article II. On matter's double causality and potency, and the eduction of forms from the potency of matter.

1. First note that matter — the material cause — has a double causality: one toward the composite or mattered thing, another toward the forms that depend on it. Toward the composite its causality lies in constituting that composite as an essential part. Toward the forms that hang on it, its causality lies in concurring passively with the agent to give them being and to keep that being.

2. Second, matter's potency is of two kinds. One is only receptive, not causative; the other is both receptive and causative. Matter has the first kind toward the rational soul alone: it can naturally receive the soul into itself, but it cannot concur as a material cause in giving the soul being. It has the second kind toward every other form, essential or accidental: it can receive them and, by passive concurrence, cooperate with the agent in producing them.

3. Third, those philosophers go wrong who explain eduction by saying the form already exists in act in the matter before generation, only hidden under the confusion of potency, and that generation merely makes it manifest — as if actual being that was concealed simply becomes clear and is led out of matter's darkness into light. That account is bad. If the form already existed in act and united with matter before generation, the composite would already exist before it was generated — which is openly absurd, since matter and form existing in act and united necessarily yield the composite. Someone will object: if the form is not in the matter beforehand, how can it be educed or drawn out of it? Nothing is drawn out of what it is not in. Reply: the form is said to be educed from matter not from matter's substance, but from matter's causative potency. Before generation it does not exist in the substance of matter, yet it truly exists in matter's potency insofar as matter can produce it as a passive principle. To be in matter's causative potency is simply to be producible by matter as a passive principle.

4. Fourth, those also are wholly wrong who say forms exist in matter before generation according to an incomplete, imperfect being — by degrees of their entity — and through generation first attain complete, finished being in matter. That view makes a substantial form vary in intensity like an accident; and it absurdly packs into one and the same matter, all at once, every form that could be educed from it, total or partial — nearly infinite diverse substantial entities in one thing. Someone will object: if the form is nothing at all before generation, then every form comes from nothing and is therefore created. Reply: forms may be said to come from nothing if that means from no pre-existing part of themselves; not if it means from no pre-existing matter, which is the same as creation. Forms come to be from matter: matter concurs as a subjective cause in giving them being.

5. Fifth, it is also a bad account of eduction to say a form is educed from matter's potency merely because matter, before the form arrives, can receive it. If that were enough, every form without exception would be educible from matter's potency, since matter can receive any form — by a natural potency or an obediential one. Natural potency can be brought into act by a natural agent: wood's passive potency for heat is natural because fire can actualize it. Obediential potency cannot be actualized by a natural agent, but only by a superior agent of another order to which the matter is so subject that it must obey: wood or stone's potency for a statue's form is of this kind (art, not nature, actualizes it); so is the soul's potency for supernatural gifts — faith, hope, charity — which no natural power can bring into act, but only the creator's infinite power.

6. With that in place, eduction is easy to state. Nothing is educed from a thing except what was already in it. So only those forms are educed from matter's causative potency that, before they exist, are in that potency — producible by matter's passive concurrence. While they do not yet exist in act they can receive being from matter as a passive, receptive principle; when they begin to exist in act by the agent's active power and matter's passive power, they are rightly said to be educed from matter's causative potency, because they are no longer producible by it. What has once been caused is no longer in the cause's potency; it has been led from potentiality into actuality. A brute's form is truly educed from the causative potency of the seed's matter: before generation it was producible by that matter's passive power; through the generator's action it is produced and set outside that potency, and is producible by it again only if it loses the existence it now has. The human soul is produced in matter, yet it is not educed from matter's causative potency; it is induced into matter. It never lay in that potency, and matter never had a power, by passive concurrence, to give the soul being.

source_text:
ART. III.
An anima rationalis sit ex traduce.

1. Verus hujus controversiae status est, utrum anima rationalis educatur ex potentia materiae seminis, vi seminalis & prolificae virtutis, sicut animae plantarum, & belluarum: an vero a DEO absque materiae praeexistentis concursu producatur, h.e. creatur, & corpori infundatur. Posterior sententia omnibus fere modernis Philosophis, & Theologis arridet, & merito; non enim memini me legisse ullum argumentum in contrarium, tanti ponderis, ut genium aliquem, vel mediocriter in hac controversia versatum, in eorum sententiam adduceret, qui contendunt animas nostras a parentibus, per carnalem generationem proseminari; non vero a DEO creari, & infundi. Contra vero, pro ea sententia, quae asserit animas humanas a DEO immediate creari, non solum faciunt varia S. Scripturae testimonia, sed etiam argumenta Philosophica principiis naturae notis nitentia: ego autem, omissis argumentis ex S. Scriptura petitis, quia ea luculenter proponuntur a Theologis, praecipue vero a clarissimo D. Junio, in explicatione 1. cap. Genes. rationes quasdam afferám, partim ex Physica, partim ex Metaphysica depromptas.

2. Prima ratio est haec: Si anima est generabilis, est corruptibilis: at absurdum est posterius: Ergo & prius: ratio majoris est haec; illa forma, quae ita dependet a materia, ut per concursum causae materialis in generatione producatur, ita etiam dependet a materia, ut si ab ea separetur, quae conferebat & conservabat ejus esse, necessario pereat. Ad hoc argumentum respondere solent Theologi, & Philosophi, qui sunt in contraria sententia, animas humanas esse ex se corruptibiles, ut probat illud argumentum; quia dependent a materia in fieri & esse, duraturas tamen esse in aeternum, quia DEUS statuit eas conservare. Quod si quis eos roget, cur anima, in se spectata, sit corruptibilis: Respondent hanc esse rationem, quia si DEUS cessaret ab actu quo conservat animas, illae statim in nihilum redirent. Sed haec responsio non placet, primo quia Theologi, & Philosophi, cum dividunt substantias in aeternas & caducas, non volunt aliquas substantias ideo esse aeternas, quod a conservativo DEI influxu non dependeant; sed quod a nulla creatura, per actionem Physicam destrui possint: hoc autem modo non solum Angeli, & Coelum, sed etiam animae rationales incorruptibiles dici possunt. Deinde illi qui ita respondent, non possunt negare animam humanam ita se habere, ut nulla actione Physica, seu materiali destrui possit: unde ego infero, eam nulla actione Physica, vel materiali, posse produci. Quaenam enim est ratio, quod nulla actione Physica destrui possit? Nonne, quia est substantia spiritualis? At ob eandem etiam rationem, nulla virtute materiali potest produci, idque quia, sicut repugnat spiritui actione Physica & materiali destrui, ita etiam repugnat spiritui actione Physica & materiali produci; generatio autem est actio Physica & materialis, tum quia fit in materia, tum quia fit per virtutem materialem, scilicet per virtutem seminalem.

3. Secunda ratio: Deus voluit animas humanas existere, extra corpora, post hominum mortem; voluit autem animas belluarum perire cum corporibus: Ergo dedit animae rationali, naturam independentem a materia, ut ratione illius naturae possit existere extra materiam corpoream; unde infero animam quoad naturam suam esse independentem a materia corporea.

4. Tertio, Ea sola forma educitur ex potentia causativa materiae, quae fit materia passive concurrente, ad tribuendum ei esse: sed materia seminis non potest concursu passivo, tribuere esse animae: Ergo non educitur ex potentia materiae, sed a Deo per creationem in materiam infunditur. Propositio manifesta est ex praecedentibus: assumptio probatur; nulla virtus activa agit ultra suum genus, ut loquuntur; i.e. non potest agendo producere eam rem, quae est excellentioris naturae, & superioris ordinis: sed anima excedit totum genus naturae corporeae, cum sit substantia spiritualis: nulla igitur virtus corporea potest animam producere. Ad hoc argumentum respondere solent, vim materialem in semine existentem per se non posse producere spiritualem substantiam animae, posse tamen virtute spiritualis illius substantiae, cujus est instrumentum, i.e. virtute animae hominis generantis, elevari ultra suam speciem, ad producendum spiritum: quemadmodum phantasma, quod est sensibilis & materialis species, virtute animae, cujus est instrumentum, species intelligibiles, h.e. spirituales rerum imagines intellectui patienti imprimit. Hoc effugium plane futile est, & nullius momenti; fieri enim non potest, ut a gente creatum opera instrumenti pure materialis, aliquid immateriale producatur; facultas autem prolifica in semine existens, pure materialis est; secus tamen accidit, in productione specierum intelligibilium; anima enim utitur vi intellectus agentis, ut principalis instrumenti, excitantis & elevantis phantasma, ad producendas illas species; quare universaliter verum est, virtutem materialem non posse esse aut principale, aut solitarium instrumentum, in productione spiritualis substantiae, licet esse possit instrumentum secundarium, in productione spiritualis qualitatis.

5. Quarto, Illi qui sunt in opposita sententia, coguntur admittere conclusiones admodum duras, & absurdas; nam ut vitent vim talium argumentorum, coguntur admittere animam non esse substantiam spiritualem; item animam posse actione Physica destrui, nisi DEUS eam speciali suo auxilio conservet ab interitu: quae conclusiones admodum derogant dignitati, & excellentiae animae nostrae, & nobis auferunt occasionem confutandi Atheos, argumentis petitis ab immortalitate animae. Si enim anima est forma natura sua dependens a corpore, ita ut extra corpus per se existere non valeat, quomodo persuadebimus iis, animam esse immortalem? derogant etiam hae conclusiones sapientiae divinae; quippe asserere DEUM voluisse animas existere, extra corpora, & negasse iis naturam ad hoc idoneam, est dicere DEUM non satis prudenter produxisse animam.

6. Quinto, Quamvis dicamus animam a DEO creari, & in corpus infundi, & proinde parentem non tribuere filio suo animam, satis tamen commode tueri possumus, hominem tam vere generare hominem, quam leo leonem, & bos bovem; possumus item tueri naturalem & hereditariam corruptionem, quam Peccatum Originale vocant, a parentibus ad liberos propagari, & hujus propagationis modum explicare: nulla ergo necessitas nos cogit amplecti eam sententiam, quae animae naturae repugnat, & ejus dignitati tantum detrahit.
english: Article III. Whether the rational soul is from a translate.

1. The real question is this: is the rational soul educed from the potency of the seed's matter by seminal and prolific power, as plant and brute souls are — or does God produce it without any concurrence of pre-existing matter, creating it and infusing it into the body? Nearly all modern philosophers and theologians favor the second view, and rightly. I do not recall any contrary argument weighty enough to pull even a moderately practiced mind into the camp of those who say our souls are sown by parents in carnal generation and not created and infused by God. For immediate creation by God, Scripture's witness and philosophical arguments from known principles of nature both count. Leaving Scripture to the theologians — especially Junius on Genesis 1 — I offer reasons drawn from physics and metaphysics.

2. First: if the soul is generable, it is corruptible; but the consequent is absurd, so the antecedent is too. A form produced in generation by matter's concurrence depends on matter so that, once separated from what gave and kept its being, it must perish. Opponents reply that human souls are of themselves corruptible — the argument shows they depend on matter in becoming and being — yet will last forever because God has decreed to conserve them. Asked why the soul considered in itself is corruptible, they say that if God stopped conserving souls they would at once sink into nothing. That answer fails. When substances are divided into eternal and perishable, eternity does not mean independence from God's conserving influx; it means no creature can destroy them by a physical action. On that score angels, the heavens, and rational souls alike may be called incorruptible. Further, those who answer so cannot deny that the human soul cannot be destroyed by any physical or material action; from which I infer it also cannot be produced by any such action. Why can no physical action destroy it? Because it is a spiritual substance. For the same reason no material power can produce it: what is repugnant to a spirit in destruction is repugnant to it in production. Generation is a physical, material action — done in matter, by seminal virtue.

3. Second: God willed human souls to exist outside bodies after death, and brute souls to perish with their bodies. Therefore he gave the rational soul a nature independent of matter, so that by that nature it can exist outside corporeal matter. As to its nature, then, the soul is independent of corporeal matter.

4. Third: only that form is educed from matter's causative potency which comes to be with matter's passive concurrence giving it being. The seed's matter cannot by passive concurrence give being to the soul. Therefore the soul is not educed from matter's potency; God creates it and pours it into matter. The major is clear from what went before. The minor: no active power acts beyond its genus — it cannot produce what is of a higher nature and order. The soul exceeds the whole order of corporeal nature as a spiritual substance; no corporeal power can produce it. They reply that the material force in the seed cannot of itself make a spiritual substance, yet can, as instrument of the generating soul, be elevated beyond its species to produce a spirit — as a phantasm, a sensible material species, by the soul's power impresses intelligible (spiritual) images on the patient intellect. That evasion is empty. A created agent cannot, by a purely material instrument, produce something immaterial; and the prolific faculty in the seed is purely material. The case of intelligible species is different: the soul uses the agent intellect as a principal instrument to excite and elevate the phantasm. Universally, a material power cannot be the principal or sole instrument in producing a spiritual substance, though it may be a secondary instrument in producing a spiritual quality.

5. Fourth: opponents are driven to hard, absurd conclusions. To dodge these arguments they must deny that the soul is a spiritual substance, and allow that a physical action can destroy it unless God specially preserves it — claims that strip our soul of dignity and leave us no purchase against atheists from immortality. If the soul by nature depends on the body so that it cannot of itself exist outside it, how shall we persuade them it is immortal? The same conclusions slight divine wisdom: to say God willed souls to exist outside bodies and yet denied them a nature fit for that is to say he did not produce the soul wisely enough.

6. Fifth: though we hold that God creates the soul and infuses it, so that the parent does not give the child a soul, we can still maintain that a human generates a human as truly as a lion a lion or an ox an ox; and we can maintain that the natural hereditary corruption called original sin is passed from parents to children, and explain how. Nothing forces us into an opinion that contradicts the soul's nature and so deeply detracts from its dignity.

ART. IV.
An & quomodo homo vere generare hominem dicatur.

1. Philosophi, & Theologi, qui dicunt animam non traduci per semen, aut ex semine elici, variis modis dissentiunt de generatione hominis, & actione in qua generatio hominis consistit. Primo enim nonnulli, cum iis hoc argumentum objicitur — homo generans non tribuit filio animam, per quam est homo: Ergo homo non generat hominem — Respondent hominem dici generare hominem, quia suppeditat materiam ex qua fit homo, id est, quia tribuit filio corpus hominis: verum haec responsio admodum frigida est & indigna quae ab ullo Philosopho proferatur: primo enim ex ea sequitur, hominem tantum generare corpus hominis, non vero totum hominem; & hoc est ipsum, quod argumentum probat. Secundo, quia nemo Philosophorum dixit, generationem substantialem esse productionem aut suppeditationem materiae; si enim producere substantiam, est suppeditare materiam ad producendam substantiam; pari ratione, is qui suppeditat artifici materiam ad conficiendam statuam, dicetur conficere statuam; quod admodum absurdum est. Tertio, generare hominem, est tribuere esse homini, ut ex ipsis terminis patet: at esse hominis seu natura humana, neque consistit in anima sola, neque in corpore solo, ut omnes fatentur: si enim natura humana in altero horum consisteret, per separationem animae a corpore non destrueretur natura humana: consistit ergo natura humana, in unione corporis & animae, i.e. consistit in eo, quod homo vere constet anima & corpore: si ergo generans non efficit, ut filius sit quid constans ex anima & corpore, sed tantum efficit ipsum corpus, homo generans non vere dicetur tribuere homini genito esse hominis, atque adeo non vere dicetur generare hominem.

2. Alii, cum vident se non posse evitare vim hujus argumenti per priorem responsionem, aliam responsionem adferunt, sed pene tam invalidam ac est prior: dicunt hominem vere generare hominem, quia non solum tribuit ei materiam, i.e. corpus; sed etiam praeparat materiam ad recipiendam formam; atque adeo per virtutem prolificam, attingit conjunctionem animae & corporis, per quam conjunctionem homo constituitur in esse hominis, & fit tale compositum Physicum: hi ergo non dicunt patrem conjungere animam filii cum corpore filii, per virtutem seminalem, (hoc enim tribuunt DEO qui animam infundit;) sed praeparare materiam seminis ad recipiendam formam humanam, quam quidem praeparationem, postquam completa fuerit, immediate sequitur conjunctio animae & corporis: hinc liquet ex eorum sententia, actionem generandi nihil aliud esse quam praeviam materiae alterationem, & praeparationem ad recipiendam formam: in hac sententia fuerunt pene omnes antiquiores Philosophi; etiam omnes pene Moderni, plerique etiam Pontificii Theologi; nam Conimbricenses, in explicatione lib. 1. de ortu, testantur se ipsos olim amplexos fuisse hanc sententiam, quia fuit recepta apud omnes: verum haec sententia, ut dictum est, non magis satisfacit argumento quam prior. Primo, quia praeparatio materiae est mutatio in qualitate, atque adeo est alteratio. Generatio autem non est alteratio; sunt enim diversi specie motus, in hoc differentes, quod altera terminetur ad qualitatem, altera ad substantiam: Ergo generatio non est mutatio, vel praeparatio materiae; neque generare, est praeparare materiam. Secundo, generatio est una simplex mutatio, vel simplex motus, ut omnes fatentur: at illa praeparatio non est posita in una mutatione, sed in variis alterationibus, quae praecedunt introductionem formae: nam aliquando dilatatur, aliquando consolidatur illa materia, aliquando humor augetur, aliquando minuitur, ita scilicet postulante natura formae introducendae: Ergo illa praeparatio non est generatio, sed aggregata, seu multiplex mutatio, sive alteratio. Tertio, generare est tribuere esse; esse autem hominis consistit in eo, quod constet ex anima & corpore: si ergo DEUS copulet animam cum corpore, infundendo (ut dicunt Theologi,) DEUS tribuit esse homini, non vero generans: solus enim ille qui copulat animam cum corpore, efficit ut homo constet ex anima & corpore. Denique homo in instanti gignitur, id est, in instanti fit homo: Ergo non gradatim; ideoque ejus productio, non est mutatio aliqua successiva, sed instantanea.

3. Tertius modus respondendi est eorum, qui dicunt hominem generare hominem, neque quod ei tribuat materiam, neque quod materiam praeparet; sed quod tribuat ei etiam formam, non quidem specificam, id est, animam rationalem (hanc enim volunt tribui a solo DEO, qui eam creat, & unit cum corpore;) sed quod ex potentia seminis educat animam vegetativam, & sensitivam: verum haec sententia minime omnium placet, quia manifeste ex ea sequitur, hominem non generare hominem, sed hoc vivens, & hoc animal; praeterea (ut dicebam) esse hominis in eo consistit, quod homo constet ex anima & corpore; Si ergo filius non debeat patri, quod constet ex anima rationali & corpore, non habet naturam hominis a patre sibi communicatam.

4. Rejectis his sententiis, nos cum doctissimis Philosophis, Du Val, Sc. Ruvio, & Professoribus Academiae Conimbricensis, quartum dicendi modum amplectimur, asserentes hominem vere generare hominem, quamvis anima a DEO creatur; non quod tribuat ei corpus solummodo, neque quod praeparet corpus ad recipiendam animam; neque quod in materia, aut ex materia corporea, efficiat animam vegetativam, aut sensitivam sui filii; sed quod ab homine generante sit ipsa actio, qua anima rationalis substantialiter corpori unitur, ac incipit informare, inhabitare, & implere totam materiam corporis: adeo ut ex nostra sententia, generatio hominis sit posita in illa actione, qua, per virtutem prolificam, anima essentiali vinculo cum corpore copulatur.
english: Article IV. Whether and how a human being is truly said to generate a human being.

1. Philosophers and theologians who deny that the soul is translated through the seed, or drawn out of it, still disagree about what human generation is and in what action it consists. Some, pressed with the objection that the generator does not give the child the soul through which he is human and therefore does not generate a human, answer that a human generates a human by supplying the matter — the body — from which the human is made. That reply is cold and unworthy of a philosopher. It yields only that a human generates a human body, not the whole human — which is exactly what the objection proves. No philosopher has made substantial generation out to be the production or supply of matter; if producing a substance were supplying matter for it, the man who hands an artisan marble for a statue would be said to make the statue — which is absurd. To generate a human is to give a human being; and human being or nature is neither soul alone nor body alone. If it were either, separating soul from body would not destroy human nature. Human nature is the union of body and soul — truly consisting of both. If the generator only makes the body and does not make the child something consisting of soul and body, he does not truly give the child human being, and so does not truly generate a human.

2. Others, seeing the first reply fails, offer another almost as weak. They say a human truly generates a human because he not only gives a body but prepares the matter to receive the form, and by prolific virtue reaches the conjunction of soul and body that constitutes a human as a physical composite. They do not say the father joins the child's soul to the body by seminal virtue — that they leave to God who infuses the soul — but that he prepares the seed's matter for the human form, after which preparation the conjunction follows at once. On their view, generating is only a prior alteration and preparation of matter. Nearly all the older philosophers held this, nearly all the moderns, and most Roman theologians; the Coimbra commentators on De ortu 1 admit they once held it because it was common. It satisfies the objection no better than the first. Preparation of matter is a change in quality — alteration — and generation is not alteration: they are specifically different motions, one ending in quality, the other in substance. So generation is not preparation of matter. Generation is one simple change; that preparation is many alterations before the form arrives — dilating, solidifying, increasing or decreasing humor as the form requires. So it is an aggregate of changes, not generation. To generate is to give being; human being is consisting of soul and body. If God couples soul and body by infusion, God gives that being, not the generator. And a human is begotten in an instant, not gradually; so production is instantaneous, not successive.

3. A third reply says the generator gives neither matter alone nor preparation alone, but also a form — not the specific rational soul (God alone creates and unites that), but a vegetative and sensitive soul educed from the seed's potency. This is the weakest view of all. It makes a human generate not a human but a living thing and an animal. Human being is consisting of soul and body; if the child does not owe the father that he consists of a rational soul and a body, human nature has not been communicated by the father.

4. Rejecting these, we follow Du Val, Ruvio, and the Coimbra professors in a fourth account: a human truly generates a human even though God creates the soul — not by giving only a body, not by preparing the body for the soul, not by producing a vegetative or sensitive soul of the child in or from corporeal matter, but because from the generator comes the very action by which the rational soul is substantially united to the body and begins to inform, inhabit, and fill the whole matter of the body. On our view, human generation is that action by which, through prolific virtue, the soul is bound to the body by an essential bond.

source_text:
ART. V.
Utrum generatio posita sit in productione formae, an vero in conjunctione formae cum materia.

1. Ut nostrae sententiae veritas appareat, primo ostendam actionem generantis (loquendo in genere, de omni generatione) esse positam in conjunctione materiae & formae: secundo, nonnihil specialius dicam de illa actione, qua anima corpori unitur. Quod ad prius attinet, generatio compositi non est productio materiae; idque quia materia proprie dicta est ingenerabilis, & incorruptibilis; h.e. a nullo potest fieri, nisi a creatore: si enim creatura aliqua produceret materiam primam, produceret eam ex nulla materia praeexistente; atque adeo crearet eam; nulla autem creatura creat, cum creatio requirat infinitam virtutem. Deinde cum ex igne fit aer, aer generat alium aerem, mutando ignem in aerem, non autem per illam generationem producit materiam novi aeris, sed in materiam praeexistentem introducit formam novi aeris.

2. Generatio substantialis, non est productio materiae, ut jam ostensum est; at neque est productio formae, quod quidem certum est, & evidens apud eos, qui dicunt animas a DEO creari: at non minus evidenter etiam probari potest contra eos, qui dicunt animam esse ex traduce. Primo enim natura hominis est in eo posita, quod constet ex anima & corpore: at per actionem qua anima unitur corpori, sive anima sit a DEO sive a patre, homo fit compositum constans ex anima & corpore: Ergo per illam actionem, homo accipit naturam, vel esse hominis; & proinde per illam actionem producitur: quid enim est aliud, producere hominem, quam efficere ut existat homo, seu Ens constans ex anima & corpore? Secundo, nunquam potest compositum Physicum de novo produci, sive per generationem, sive per aliam mutationem, nisi ejus materia & forma de novo conjungantur, & coeant in unum per se, ut evidens est: potest tamen compositum Physicum de novo produci, & revera fieri, quamvis ejus forma non producatur de novo: Ergo efficere compositum Physicum, potius est materiam & formam conjungere, quam formam producere: probatur assumptio; primo, ex resurrectione mortuorum in die judicii: tum enim homines de novo producentur, & de novo accipient esse hominis, per veram productionem substantialem, licet non ordinariam, sed plane extraordinariam; at tum eorum anima non potest dici de novo produci, quia existabat semper postquam creata est; sed tantum de novo uniri cum materia: Ergo productio compositi Physici non est productio formae, sed potius unitio formae cum materia. Si quis tam impudens sit, ut neget in resurrectione mortuorum fieri veram productionem substantialem, contra eum utar hoc argumento; Producere substantiam corpoream, est tribuere esse substantiae corporeae: at tum DEUS hominibus mortuis, qui quamdiu mortui erant non habebant verum esse substantiae naturalis, quia non constabant ex materia & forma unitis, vere & proprie dabit integrum & plenum esse corporis naturalis, efficiendo ut vere constent ex corpore & anima: Ergo DEUS per illam actionem vere producit corpora naturalia. Non negari quidem potest, illam actionem esse actionem longe diversam a generatione substantiali, & modo generandi ordinario; certum tamen est eam actionem esse veram productionem substantialem; quod probamus ex definitione productionis substantialis; quid enim aliud est producere substantiam, quam conferre esse illi substantiae, quae ante illam actionem, non habebat esse substantiale. Secundo probatur assumptio sic; DEUS potest creare animam infantis per aliquod tempus ante ejus generationem, & postea, in ipsa generatione, illam animam cum corpore ejus conjungere: Ergo potest esse vera generatio substantialis absque productione formae.

3. Quod ad posterius attinet: Theologi & Philosophi, qui sunt in nostra sententia de origine animae, afferunt virtutem seminalem in belluis duplicem habere operationem; scilicet eductionem formae ex potentia materiae, & unitionem ejusdem formae cum composito; quas quidem actiones dicunt non realiter sed ratione sola diversas esse: idque quia per unam & eandem actionem educitur forma ex potentia materiae, & unitur substantialiter cum materia. Contra, afferunt virtutem seminalem, quae in semine hominis existit, habere unam tantum actionem; scilicet unitionem formae, i.e. animae cum materia corporea; unam (inquam) actionem principalem, nam certum est, ab ea virtute proficisci varias actiones minus principales, scil. praeparationes materiae corporeae ad recipiendam animam: quare dicunt in productione hominis esse duas actiones proficiscentes a diversis agentibus; scilicet creationem animae, & unitionem ejusdem cum materia: creationem animae aiunt esse operationem solius DEI, quod evidens est; unitionem vero animae cum corpore, volunt esse actionem, non quidem solius hominis; DEUS enim cooperatur cum homine in actione illa; sed hominis & DEI simul: & addunt, in hac unitione, & non in alia actione, positam esse generationem hominis: quod ex eo patet, quia supra ostensum est, producere compositum, neque esse producere materiam, neque producere formam, sed formam cum materia unire, & copulare; ex nostra ergo sententia, eodem instanti, quo DEUS creat animam in corpore, homo generans per virtutem seminalem animam a DEO creatam cum corpore, substantialiter unit, & connectit; adeo ut actio DEI terminetur ad animae esse simpliciter; actio vero patris terminetur, non quidem ad animae esse simpliciter, sed ad ejus esse in corpore, seu ad unionem animae cum corpore.

4. Ad illud argumentum, homo est homo per animam; si ergo pater non tribuit filio animam, non tribuit ei esse hominem. Respondent, hominem esse hominem, neque per animam seorsim acceptam, neque per corpus, sed per integram naturam, sive per essentiam humanam; & aiunt patrem uniendo animam cum corpore, per virtutem seminalem tribuere filio το συνεστάναι ex anima & corpore; & proinde ei tribuere naturam & essentiam per quam est homo; patet autem unamquamque rem, esse talem rem non per alteram essentiae partem, sed per totam essentiam, quia essentia est id, per quod Ens est Ens; atque adeo talis essentia est id, per quod res est talis res: illud autem quod dici solet, unamquamque rem esse talem rem per formam suam, ita concipiendum est ut intelligamus unamquamque rem esse talem rem per formam, non quidem tanquam adaequatam rationem (ratio enim adaequata cur res sit talis res, est quia habet talem essentiam) sed tanquam principalem partem essentiae; si enim inter se conferamus partes essentiae Physicae, res quaelibet est talis res per formam, potius quam per materiam; interim si conferamus aut formam, aut materiam cum integra essentia, res quaelibet est talis res potius per essentiam, quam aut per materiam, aut formam.

5. Verum, hic oritur magna difficultas; si enim DEUS infundit animam, (ut omnes Theologi loquuntur, qui sunt in hac sententia) conjunctio animae cum corpore potius tribuenda erit DEO, quam homini generanti; quid enim aliud est animae infusio in materiam corpoream, quam conjunctio animae cum materia? Respondent nonnulli DEUM dici infundere animam, non quod per se solum copulet animam cum corpore; sed quod per virtutem seminalem illud praestet, cujus ministerio utitur tanquam instrumento, non quidem necessario (ipse enim potest per se connectere animam & corpus.) sed ordinario, quia scilicet ejus usus est ordinarius in omni animalium generatione. Alii probabilius respondent, Deum dici infundere animam in corpus, non quod substantialiter, sed quod localiter conjungat animam & corpus: id est, quod creat animam in corpore, & per ejus creationem in tali ubi, efficiat eam localiter praesentem corpori: dicunt enim, eodem instanti quo DEUS creat animam localiter praesentem corpori, eodem (inquam) instanti virtutem seminalem eas partes connectere, vinculo substantiali: docent autem localem praesentiam animae, esse quid longe diversum ab ejus unione substantiali cum materia; quia Angelus assumpto corpore vestitus, est localiter praesens illi corpori, non vero substantialiter ei conjunctus, ut forma materiae suae.
english: Article V. Whether generation is placed in the production of the form or in the conjunction of form with matter.

1. To make our view clear I will first show that the generator's action — speaking of generation in general — is placed in the conjunction of matter and form; then I will say something more particular about the action that unites soul and body. Generation of a composite is not production of matter. Matter properly so called is ingenerable and incorruptible: only the creator can make it. If a creature produced prime matter from no pre-existing matter, it would create it; no creature creates, for creation needs infinite power. When air comes from fire, air generates air by turning fire into air; it does not produce new matter, but introduces a new form into matter already there.

2. Substantial generation is not production of matter, as shown; nor is it production of form. That is clear for those who hold souls are created by God, and no less clear against traducians. First: human nature is consisting of soul and body. By the action that unites soul to body — whether the soul is from God or from the father — a human becomes a composite of soul and body. So by that action the human receives human being and is produced: to produce a human is to bring it about that a being consisting of soul and body exists. Second: a physical composite is never produced anew — by generation or any other change — unless matter and form are newly joined into one per se. Yet a physical composite can be produced anew even when its form is not newly produced. So making a physical composite is joining matter and form rather than producing the form. Proof from the resurrection: then humans will be newly produced and newly receive human being by a true substantial production, though extraordinary; yet their soul is not newly produced — it has existed since creation — but only newly united with matter. So production of a physical composite is uniting form with matter, not producing form. If anyone denies that the resurrection is a true substantial production: to produce a corporeal substance is to give it being; God then truly gives the dead — who while dead lacked the being of a natural substance, not consisting of united matter and form — the full being of a natural body by making them consist of body and soul. So by that action God truly produces natural bodies. The action differs from ordinary generation, yet it is a true substantial production: to produce a substance is to confer being on what did not have substantial being before. Further: God can create an infant's soul some time before generation and then, in generation itself, join that soul to the body. So there can be true substantial generation without producing the form.

3. On the second point: those of our opinion on the soul's origin say that in brutes the seminal virtue has a double operation — educing the form from matter's potency, and uniting that form with the composite — operations diverse only in reason, because one and the same action educes the form and substantially unites it with matter. In humans, they say, the seminal virtue has only one principal action: uniting the form — the soul — with corporeal matter (lesser actions of preparing the body for the soul also proceed from it). So in producing a human there are two actions from two agents: creation of the soul, and uniting it with matter. Creation is God's alone. Uniting soul and body is not the human's alone — God cooperates — but the human's and God's together. And generation is placed in that uniting, not in another action: as shown, producing a composite is neither producing matter nor producing form, but uniting form with matter. In the same instant God creates the soul in the body, the generating human by seminal virtue substantially joins the God-created soul to the body. God's action terminates in the soul's being simply; the father's terminates not in that simple being but in the soul's being in the body — the union of soul and body.

4. To the objection that a human is human through the soul, so if the father does not give a soul he does not give human being: they reply that a human is human neither through soul alone nor through body alone, but through the whole nature or human essence. By uniting soul and body through seminal virtue the father gives the child to consist of soul and body, and so gives the nature and essence through which he is human. A thing is such a thing through the whole essence, not through one part — for essence is that through which a being is a being. The common saying that each thing is such through its form means: through the form as the principal part of the essence, not as an adequate reason (the adequate reason is having such an essence). Comparing the parts of a physical essence, a thing is such through form rather than matter; comparing either part with the whole essence, it is such through the essence rather than through either matter or form alone.

5. A serious difficulty remains. If God infuses the soul, as all of this opinion say, the conjunction of soul and body seems God's rather than the generator's — for what is infusion into corporeal matter but conjunction with matter? Some answer that God is said to infuse the soul not because he alone couples them, but because he does it through seminal virtue used as an instrument — not a necessary instrument (he can connect them of himself) but an ordinary one, as in every animal generation. Others more probably say God is said to infuse the soul not by substantially but by locally joining soul and body: he creates the soul in the body and by creating it in that place makes it locally present. In that same instant the seminal virtue connects the parts by a substantial bond. Local presence of the soul is far different from substantial union with matter: an angel clothed in an assumed body is locally present to that body, yet not substantially joined to it as form to its matter.
